accuracy.evidence: Rules match the National Curriculum English Appendix 2: Year 1 capital letters plus full stop, question mark or exclamation mark; capitals for names and I; Year 2 statement, question, exclamation and command. Exclamation examples were rewritten to the STA test form (What or How plus a verb: What a big cake this is!) after checking the KS1 GPS framework, so the lab never teaches a fragment as the model exclamation.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented KS1 slips: a capital on every word or mid-sentence (cat tap feedback), a full stop at the end of a line instead of the idea (The sun is. stops too soon), a full stop on a question, What-starting exclamations read as questions, and run-on lines with no boundary (We went to the park we fed the ducks).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagstop is built around sentence boundaries: word tiles with tappable gaps, a draggable full-stop chip that is judged by where it lands, an end slot that takes . ? or ! and shows a telling/asking/big-feeling face, and a run-on splitter that inserts the stop and capitalises the next word. flagsent (building sentences) only adds a capital and stop at the end; the shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each rule by acting: tapping cat gives a reason why only the first word is capital, dropping the stop after is reads back The sun is. as unfinished, and the mood face after each mark ties the mark to what the sentence does. Splitting run-ons shows a full stop and a capital always come together.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with a tempting wrong option: Every word (capital), a full stop for Where is my hat, and a question mark for What a big cake this is. Each task right after the prediction makes the learner test it, and the done message says whether the guess held.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged messages, each naming the slip: no capital (The, not the), no end mark, full stop on an Is-it question, shouting mark on a question, What-exclamation read as a question, run-on I ran I won, missing capital on the second sentence, capital in the middle (hat), capital on every word.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores FK 0.5 against the family limit of 5.0, with three- to eight-word sentences and examples in every paragraph. Adult text scores FK 6.5 against the limit of 10, uses the curriculum terms statement, question, exclamation, command, capital letter, full stop, question mark and exclamation mark, and names the tests the terms come from.

no_filler.evidence: No stock phrases; the filler gate passed. Every kid paragraph has a rule and a worked sentence; adult paragraphs give curriculum, the teaching distinction, the common mistakes and what the lab does. The explanation overlaps other lessons by less than 12%.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark show word tiles at 20 px, mark chips 56 px square, and wrapped lines with no clipping. Pointer tests on the iPhone viewport placed the full stop by drag (wrong drop after is gave the too-soon message; drop at the end worked), tapped words for capitals and split a run-on by tapping park.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs axe run found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme on desktop or iPhone. Every canvas action has a button: one per word for the capital and the stop, three labelled end-mark buttons, and stop-after buttons for the splitter. The canvas aria-label reads each result aloud.

sources: DfE (2013) English programmes of study KS1-2, Appendix 2: vocabulary, grammar and punctuation (Years 1-2)
STA Key stage 1 English grammar, punctuation and spelling test framework (exclamation sentences: What or How plus a verb)
Common Core State Standards ELA L.K.2, L.1.2
